summary: Defines a new LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV for the PCEP LSP object. The original Flag field is only 12 bits, and all of them were already assigned, so this gives a place for more flags.

plainLanguage.summary: A form ran out of checkboxes, so this adds a second page with more checkboxes.

questions: what to do when pcep lsp flags are full
what is the pcep lsp-extended-flag tlv
why was the pcep lsp flag field extended
what is tlv type 64 in pcep
subtitle: Adds a variable-length extended flag field to the PCEP LSP object after its 12 original flag bits ran out.

tldr.problem: The LSP object in the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) has a Flag field of 12 bits, and every one of those bits is already assigned.
tldr.mechanism: A new LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV (type 64) carries an array of 32-bit flag units, so future documents can define more flags. This RFC defines no flags itself.
tldr.outcome: PCEP gains room for new LSP flags without a new TLV each time. Implementations that do not know the TLV or a given flag ignore it. It has since been updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 9357 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9756. It defines the extended flag container only, and the text says the bits will be assigned by future documents.

sections.title: Why the Flag Field Ran Out
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) is used between a PCE and a Path Computation Client (PCC), or another PCE, to compute Label Switched Paths (LSPs) for MPLS Traffic Engineering. RFC 8231 added extensions for a stateful PCE, including the LSP object, which has a Flag field whose bits signal things such as delegation, synchronization and removal.

That Flag field is 12 bits long, and the RFC's Table 1 shows that all 12 are assigned: PCE-allocation, ERO-compression, Fragmentation, P2MP, Create, a 3-bit Operational value, Administrative, Remove, SYNC and Delegate. This document gives the LSP object a place for more flags by defining a new LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The little row of on/off switches on the LSP object is full. Every switch already does a job, so there is nowhere to add a new one.

sections.title: The LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV
sections.content:
The TLV follows the normal PCEP TLV layout from RFC 5440: a 16-bit Type, a 16-bit Length, then the value. The type is 64. The Length is the size of the value in bytes, and it MUST be a multiple of 4 and greater than 0.

The value is the LSP Extended Flags field: an array of 32-bit units, with bits numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero. Each bit stands for one LSP flag, covering an operation, a feature or a state. The field SHOULD use only as much space as it needs. Currently no bits are assigned.

As an example of a future user, the RFC mentions an E-flag requested for entropy label configuration in a separate Internet-Draft.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra page is a list of switches stored in groups of 32. You only attach as many groups as you really need.

sections.title: How Receivers Process It
sections.content:
This document does not define any flags. Future documents will assign bits. Until then, two rules govern behavior. A sender MUST set to zero any flag it does not support. A receiver MUST ignore any flag it does not understand. Unassigned bits are zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

Because the length can vary, PCEP peers MUST handle different lengths of the TLV. If a speaker receives a TLV longer than it supports, it MUST ignore the bits beyond that length. If the TLV is shorter than the implementation supports, it MUST act as if the missing bits were not set.

The Management Considerations section adds that an implementation receiving set flags it does not recognize MAY log this, which could help diagnose backward compatibility problems with future features.
sections.plainLanguage: If you get a longer list than you know about, ignore the extra switches. If you get a shorter list, pretend the missing switches are off.

sections.title: Advice for Defining New Flags
sections.content:
Following the model in Section 3.1 of RFC 8786, the RFC advises how later specifications should define additional flags. Each one is expected to describe how the new flags interact with existing flags, including what to do when both new and preexisting flags are set. They are also expected to discuss any security implications of the additional flags.

Appendix A records why the field is variable length rather than fixed at 32 bits. The working group noted that 32 bits would last quite a while, but a variable length that is a multiple of 32 bits means flags never run out and no further TLV needs defining. It also notes that RFC 5088 and RFC 5089 take the same approach for the PCE-CAP-FLAGS sub-TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who adds a new switch has to explain how it plays with the old switches. The list can grow forever, so nobody has to build a third page later.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC says the new TLV does not introduce backward compatibility issues. An implementation that does not understand the TLV MUST ignore it, as RFC 5440 already requires. Any bits in the TLV that an implementation does not understand MUST also be ignored.

Future documents that define bits are expected to define the error handling for the case where the TLV is missing but MUST be present, and to take the ignoring rule into account.
sections.plainLanguage: Old devices just skip the new page, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA allocated value 64 for LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG in the PCEP TLV Type Indicators registry. It also created the LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV Flag Field registry within the Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) Numbers registry. New values there are assigned by Standards Action (RFC 8126).

Each bit is tracked by bit number (counting from bit 0 as the most significant), capability description and reference. No values are currently defined: bits 0-31 are initially marked Unassigned, and bits above 31 will be added in future documents if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: A public notebook keeps track of which switch means what. For now every line in it says unassigned.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document does not change the security considerations of RFC 8231 for PCEP with a stateful PCE, and it raises no additional security issues beyond those in the documents it references. Any future document that specifies new flags must discuss their security implications.

RFC 8231 recommends that stateful PCEP be authenticated and encrypted using TLS (RFC 8253), following the recommendations in RFC 9325. If that is followed, the flags are protected by TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The new page changes nothing about locking the mailbox. The same lock protects it, and new switches must explain any new risks.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the value in bytes; a multiple of 4 and greater than 0.

fields.name: LSP Extended Flags
fields.desc: One or more 32-bit units of flags, numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero.
